title: Control Plane Constraint Surge — Runbook Sketch and First-Response Log
body:
Summary:
A P0-level degradation affecting hosted-api streaming and short-lived chat sessions began 2029-06-05 03:08 UTC. Symptom set: large spike in 5xx from stream brokers, elevated p99/p999 TTFB on streaming connections, and progressive eviction spikes from KV cache nodes. Incident window ~03:08–04:12 UTC with residual elevated error-rate until mitigations fully applied at 04:40 UTC. Impact: ~18% of streaming sessions experienced fragmentation or 5xx; non-streaming generation endpoints saw degraded tail latency (~+300ms p99) for a small fraction of requests due to shared routing and prefix-cache churn. No data loss.

Detection and initial signal:
- 03:07 UTC: Alert: streaming-edge-5xx-rate surge (>5x baseline) fired (oncall SLO watch). Simultaneous increase in stream-session-reconnect metric.
- Pager notified SRE oncall (rotation: priya.nair). Slack channel #oncall-hostedapi-ops annotated by edge telemetry.
- Early hypothesis in first 8 minutes: edge-side congestion or network blips.

Chronological timeline (not exhaustive):
- 03:08 UTC: Oncall begins live triage. Trending graphs show rapid increase in lease-retry counts for KV leaders, and controller-controlplane-events emitted a high rate of "policy-enforce" events for a recently toggled capacity-guard (feature flag: controlplane.v2.capacity-guard).
- 03:12 UTC: Attempts to scale edge proxies up (standard runbook step) had limited effect — ephemeral headroom exhausted. Autoscaler metrics showed multiple pools in cooldown; policy enforcement prevented immediate scale-up of a subset of control-plane managed worker pools.
- 03:18 UTC: Partial mitigation: temporarily disabled the recently rolled capacity-guard flag (roles: platform-controlplane-admin). Error rate fell quickly from 18% to ~8% over 6 minutes but tail latency remained elevated.
- 03:30 UTC: Observed cascading KV cache evictions across multiple regions. Root cause signal: a pattern of aggressive hedging from edge proxies increasing concurrent prefix requests, which caused KV lease contention and central metadata controller overload.
- 03:36 UTC: Manual open of a dedicated fallback route to a legacy serving pool (dedicated fallback pool) for highest-priority tenants, restoring most critical traffic paths.
- 03:45 UTC: Autoscaler cooldown policy adjusted to allow forced scale-up for affected pools; additional capacity provisioned.
- 04:12 UTC: Streaming 5xx rate back within non-critical thresholds; mitigation steps continue to reduce residual latency.
- 04:40 UTC: Final rollback and stabilization completed; monitoring into steady state. Post-incident review schedule set.

Immediate mitigations performed (ordered):
1) Toggle off controlplane.v2.capacity-guard (03:18 UTC) — quick partial recovery.
2) Apply emergency rate-limits on edge hedging (03:20 UTC) to reduce concurrent prefix queries per session.
3) Re-route critical tenants to dedicated fallback pool (03:36 UTC).
4) Force autoscaler exceptions for affected pools and increase pool target sizes (03:45 UTC).
5) Rebalance KV leases and increase lease TTL on high-churn prefixes (03:52 UTC).

Root cause hypothesis (synthesized):
Primary sequence that led to outage:
- A recent control plane rollout introduced a capacity-guard enforcement that attempted to prevent oversubscription by rejecting scale requests when an internal headroom metric fell below a threshold.
- The enforcement interacted poorly with the autoscaler's cooldown window: when several worker pools hit transient load, control plane rejected the autoscaler's scale-up attempts for a 30s window, causing the autoscaler to hedge by increasing concurrent client-side fallbacks (edge-side hedging).
- Hedging amplified concurrent prefix lookups and cache misses, which increased metadata controller load and triggered KV cache eviction churn across the serving layer. Lease contention and eviction pressure resulted in a feedback loop: more hedging → more cache misses → higher controller load → slower lease renewals → more hedging.
- Secondary contributor: a recent perf regression in the metadata controller's lease reaper path (merged in runtime PR #4192) made eviction and lease-handling more CPU-intensive under spiky metadata request rates, lowering the threshold at which the cascade began.

Why previous safeguards didn't catch it earlier:
- The capacity-guard rollout lacked a canary traffic policy that would have limited enforcement to low-traffic TZ windows. Its telemetry was routed to an experimental metrics sink that isn't part of the SRE dashboard.
- Autoscaler health signals assume control plane acceptance of scale requests; there was no circuit-breaker when scale requests were consistently rejected.
- Hedging limits live at edge proxies but are permissive; they adapt to perceived latency and absence of a direct control-plane rejection signal, so they increased concurrency aggressively.

Metrics and queries to reproduce (examples):
- streaming_edge_5xx_rate / rate(streaming_edge_5xx_total[1m])
- kv_cache_evictions_total by (region, prefix)
- controlplane_policy_enforce_events_count{policy="capacity-guard"} / increase(controlplane_policy_enforce_events_total[5m])
- autoscaler_scale_rejected_total{reason="controlplane_reject"}
- PromQL to detect pattern: increase(controlplane_policy_enforce_events_total[5m]) > 50 and rate(streaming_edge_5xx_total[1m]) > 0.05

Draft runbook (first-response):
Purpose: provide deterministic steps for an oncall engineer to break the feedback loop and restore streaming SLOs. This is an abbreviated playbook to be formalized.
Pre-reqs: ability to toggle control-plane feature flags, run autoscaler override, open fallback pool routes, access to KV lease rebalancer tooling.
Steps: 
A) Immediate:
  1. Confirm alert and grab primary graphs (5xx, p99 TTFB, kv-evictions, policy-enforce events, autoscaler rejections).
  2. If controlplane policy-enforce events spike and autoscaler rejections are non-zero -> proceed to B.
B) Break feedback loop:
  1. Toggle off capacity-guard feature flag (document identity of toggle and timestamp).
  2. Apply edge-side hedging cap: set max-concurrent-prefix-hedges=2 for offending edge pool(s).
  3. Open dedicated fallback route for top-tier tenants.
C) Recovery & capacity:
  1. Force autoscaler exceptions and bump pool targets for affected pools (with audit comments).
  2. Trigger KV lease-rebalance on high churn prefixes.
  3. Monitor for eviction decline for 10 minutes and for p99 TTFB to normalize.
D) If toggle rollback does not improve within 10 minutes: escalate to platform-controlplane team and prepare to rollback control-plane deployment entirely.

Post-incident actions (owner -> due):
- Platform: Add a canary gating policy for capacity-guard deployments and route its telemetry to SRE dashboard (Samir Gupta -> 2029-06-20).
- Runtime: Revert or optimize PR #4192 controller lease reaper perf regression; provide benchmark (Lina Park -> 2029-06-14).
- SRE: Implement autoscaler rejection circuit-breaker and alert on sustained rejections (Ethan Morales -> 2029-06-10).
- Edge: Harden hedging default caps and expose hedging metrics per pool (ownership: Edge team -> 2029-06-18).
- SRE + Platform: Create a golden canary job that simulates hedging + small-scale metadata load to detect cascade risks in pre-prod (Priya Nair -> 2029-06-25).

Monitoring and alerting changes proposed:
- New composite alert: controlplane.capacity-guard-enforce + autoscaler.rejection_rate high -> P1.
- Add SLO guard: when kv_cache_evictions_total rate increases 3x baseline and streaming_5xx_rate > threshold, automatically throttle hedging at the edge for the pool.
- Dashboards: Add capacity-guard telemetry widget to hosted-api SRE dashboard.

Open questions / uncertain items to investigate:
- Precise microsecond timing and causal ordering between autoscaler scale requests and controlplane rejects. Need controlplane audit logs correlated at request-id level.
- The exact cost profile of the lease reaper regression under the metadata spike — does it amplify other clusters similarly?
- Whether hedging aggressiveness can be safely reduced without regression to client-visible tail-latency for some workloads.

Notes to the oncall who handled this (tactical learnings):
- When seeing combined spikes of autoscaler.rejections and policy-enforce events, toggle scope is often the fastest path to break the loop. Document toggle name and who toggled it.
- Prefer forced scale-up and fallback routing over immediate broad rate-limits for customers with reserved SLAs.
- Keep a short written log in the incident channel with every manual scale/route toggle and timestamp.

Next steps for this doc:
- Convert to formal postmortem once runtime/plat investigations confirm root cause (deadline: 2029-06-08).
- Author formal runbook with step-by-step CLI commands and playbook automation snippets (owner: Priya Nair -> 2029-06-10).
- Schedule a cross-team blameless postmortem review meeting (invites: Platform, Runtime, Edge, SRE) for 2029-06-11.

Appendix: quick references and CLI examples (to be expanded in final runbook):
- Toggle flag: platform-cli flags set controlplane.v2.capacity-guard=false --who="oncall-sre" --reason="emergency mitigation 2029-06-05"
- Force autoscaler override: autoscaler-cli pool-scale-override --pool=hosted-streaming-xx --target=+30% --duration=30m --note="emergency"
- Rebalance leases: kvctl rebalance --prefix="top-prefix" --concurrency=4

End of draft. Please add comments/edits inline. This draft intentionally leaves exact CLI artifacts and detection thresholds configurable pending small-runbook QA.
